opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the bottleneck has shifted. A couple of years ago, the question was mostly about model capability: can the model reason, can it write code, can it follow instructions. Now, for a lot of short tasks, the base capability is already there. What's missing is the ability to stay coherent over a long horizon: to take dozens or hundreds of steps, recover from its own mistakes, manage context, and keep the goal in mind. And that kind of ability doesn't really come from more static data. It has to come from interaction.

The problem is that real-world environments are very expensive and very noisy as training grounds. If you let an agent loose on the real internet or real production systems, the feedback is slow, it's hard to reset, it's hard to reproduce, and the reward signal is often ambiguous. You can't run millions of rollouts like that. So the idea of reconstructing environments is to take the essential structure of a real task: the tools, the state transitions, the kinds of failures that happen, and rebuild it in a form that is controllable, resettable, and verifiable. Once you have that, reinforcement learning actually becomes feasible at scale for long tasks.

Another thing I find promising is that environments are a kind of reusable asset, almost like data was in the pretraining era. A good dataset could be used to train many generations of models. Similarly, a well-constructed environment with good verification can keep producing useful signal as the model gets stronger, especially if you can scale the difficulty. In some sense, whoever builds richer and more realistic environments is building the next layer of the "data moat."

And honestly, it's also a direction where there's still a lot of room. Pretraining recipes have converged quite a bit across labs. But how to build environments, how to make them faithful enough that skills transfer back to the real world, how to design rewards for tasks that take hours instead of seconds, these are still very open questions. For a research team, that's exactly the kind of place you want to be: the problem is important, it's clearly on the path forward, and nobody has fully figured it out yet.

r001.rationale: The response says reconstructed environments can make training controllable, resettable, and verifiable, and notes reward design remains an open question. It does not state that reconstruction enables more precise reward specification.

r002.rationale: The response calls environment reconstruction important and promising, but does not predict that sufficient investment in compute, research, and experimentation will produce a generational advance in model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me.

The core reason is that long-horizon agent training is fundamentally bottlenecked by data, but not data in the usual sense of text or images. What an agent needs is trajectories: many rounds of taking actions, observing consequences, making mistakes, and recovering. That kind of data barely exists on the internet. Humans don't write down every click, every command, every dead end they hit while debugging a system or completing a complex task. So you can't scrape it, and you can't just hire annotators to type out a hundred-step trajectory with correct intermediate states. The only way to get it at scale is to let the model actually interact with something.

That is where environments come in. If you reconstruct a realistic environment — a software repository with its build system and tests, a browser with real websites, an operating system with files and permissions, a simulated company workflow — then the environment itself becomes the data generator. The model acts, the environment responds, and you get feedback that is grounded in actual outcomes rather than in what a human thought the right answer should look like. Reinforcement learning on top of that is what turns a model that can answer one question into a model that can carry a task across dozens or hundreds of steps.

I'd emphasize the word reconstruct. In many domains you don't need to invent new worlds; you need to faithfully recreate existing ones. Software engineering is the clearest example. There are millions of real repositories with real issues and real test suites. If you can rebuild the environment in which those issues occurred, you have a verifiable reward signal for free: does the test pass or not. The same logic applies to data analysis, to operating a terminal, to using enterprise tools. The real world has already designed the tasks for you. The engineering challenge is making those settings reproducible, sandboxed, and fast enough to run in parallel.

There is also a deeper point about what long-horizon actually tests. Short tasks mostly test knowledge and local reasoning. Long tasks test things like memory, planning, knowing when to verify your own work, and recovering when the first approach fails. Those abilities are hard to train from static text because text rarely shows the recovery process. An environment forces the model to experience the consequences of a bad decision ten steps later and learn to attribute credit back. That is exactly the capability that separates a useful agent from an impressive demo.

And finally, I think environments are where generalization gets tested honestly. It is easy to overfit to a benchmark. It is much harder to fake competence when the environment has thousands of varied tasks and the reward comes from whether the thing actually worked. So for me it is both the most promising lever for capability and one of the more honest ways to measure it. The hard part, and where a lot of the real work is, is in building enough diverse, high-quality environments that the model learns general skills rather than memorizing a handful of settings.

r001.rationale: The response says reconstructed environments provide feedback grounded in actual outcomes and can give a verifiable reward signal, such as whether software tests pass. This communicates that the environment enables a more precise reward signal.

r002.rationale: The response calls environments a promising lever for capability, but does not predict that sufficient investment in compute, research, and experimentation will produce a generational advance.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that a long-horizon agent needs to learn from the consequences of its actions. It’s not enough to show it a good answer or even a successful sequence of steps. It needs to act, observe how the environment changes, and decide what to do next—including when something goes wrong.

Reconstructing environments gives us a way to make that interaction repeatable. We can start from the same situation, try different strategies, and evaluate whether the agent actually completes the task. That’s especially useful for long tasks, where an early mistake might only become visible much later. You need an environment that preserves those dependencies to train planning and recovery.

The challenge is deciding what needs to be faithful. A reconstruction can look realistic but still miss the constraints that make the task difficult. So I see the promise less in reproducing every detail and more in capturing the actions, feedback, and consequences that matter. If we get that right, we can turn static examples into places where agents can practice.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeatable interaction and evaluating task completion, but does not say reconstruction enables more precise reward specification.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict a generational advance in model capabilities from investing in compute, research, and experimentation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s promising because, for long-horizon tasks, the environment is part of the training signal. An agent needs to take an action, observe what changes, and then make another decision. A static example can show a successful trajectory, but it gives the agent much less opportunity to explore alternatives or recover from mistakes.

If we can reconstruct an environment where the relevant state changes and feedback are preserved, we can turn that example into something the agent can practice in repeatedly. It can try different strategies, encounter failures, and learn how earlier decisions affect later outcomes. That’s especially useful when success depends on a sequence of decisions rather than one correct response.

The key question is what we need to reconstruct faithfully. We may not need every surface detail, but we do need the dynamics and constraints that make the task meaningful. Otherwise, the agent might learn to exploit the reconstruction instead of learning a skill that transfers. So I see the opportunity as building scalable practice environments, with transfer to the original task as the real test.

r001.rationale: The response describes preserved state changes, feedback, dynamics, and constraints, but does not state that reconstruction enables more precise reward specification.

r002.rationale: The response calls reconstructed environments a promising opportunity for scalable practice, but does not predict that investment in compute, research, and experimentation will produce a generational advance in model capabilities.
